records.name: Turkey
records.summary: Turkey presents real, structured danger for trans visitors — institutionalised, presidential-level hostility that has become state policy. Police profile and detain trans women for identity checks (20 detained in Istanbul in July 2025), trans women have historically been frequent targets of torture and ill-treatment by police, and a trans woman attacked with a knife was herself detained (victim-criminalised). Transphobic attacks and Pride-event violence are documented, and foreign visitors must carry original passports at all times — creating outing risk at the frequent transit checkpoints. A draft law leaked in October 2025 would criminalise LGBT people — not yet passed but under active government consideration. The risk is concentrated in urban trans-visible contexts (Istanbul's Beyoğlu/Tarlabaşı) rather than package-holiday tourist zones, but the institutional hostility pervades.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (29 Oct 2025): a draft legislative package would effectively criminalise LGBT people under vague claims of protecting 'the family' and 'public morals' — framing the Erdoğan government has repeatedly used to legitimise stigmatisation; sets the reform backdrop as authoritarian drift. Key legislative-risk evidence for 2025-26.

Kaos GL (Feb 2026): the LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 records 313 violations in 2025 — about two-and-a-half times 2024 — dominated by detention (299 detention decisions: 256 on record, 43 off the record), plus systematic privacy attacks; frames hostility turned into state policy. Quantified annual evidence.

bianet (Aug 2025): Istanbul police detain ~20 trans women for ID checks amid profiling concerns - stopped on the street, while shopping or in cafés in Beyoğlu, held at Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station and released after 'General Information Gathering' (GBT) background checks; legal experts argue GBT checks violate ECHR Article 5; one detainee: 'They didn't fine us, but they documented us. The new law hasn't even passed yet, but they're already enforcing it on us.'

Turkish Minute (26 Feb 2026): covers the Kaos GL 2025 report — hundreds of cases documented via media monitoring and civil-society complaints; six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings; transgender individuals disproportionately affected. Second reporting of the annual data.

Truth Justice Memory Center (Aug 2025): monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week — violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025; senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepened homophobia and transphobia, and discrimination against LGBTI+ people and their allies was entrenched. Event-monitoring evidence.

Kaos GL (Sept 2025): a new Health Ministry regulation risks profiling trans people — after a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular added 'gender reassignment' to official reasons for medical-board reports, hospitals were barred from the 'other' option and told to issue e-reports, with online framing contested as an 'LGBT opening'. Transition-access regulatory drift.

Kaos GL (Aug 2024): trans woman Yaşam was knifed by a 17-year-old in Bakırköy; the perpetrator was released while the victim was referred for arrest — activists call the detention asymmetry evidence of a state hate policy. Concrete 2024 violence + policing-asymmetry case.

Nomad Lawyer (2026): Turkey's passport-carrying rule for foreigners — original photo ID required at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, with fines up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and detention warnings. Direct visitor-facing document-risk evidence.

records.name: Norway
records.summary:
Norway is very safe for trans visitors, with strong legal protections and official responses, but with a more acute violence context than its Nordic neighbours. There is no criminalisation, bathrooms are unrestricted, and the Schengen border poses no trans-specific friction; anti-discrimination law covers gender identity; and the police operate a dedicated hate-crime unit with the security service providing annual Pride threat assessments.

Offsetting facts: a terrorist shot and killed two people at Oslo Pride in 2022 (the perpetrator, an ISIS sympathiser, was sentenced to 30 years); police-reported hate crimes against queer and trans people rose sharply in 2023 (up 18% overall, with trans-specific reports nearly doubling); and though the security service reports a significant decline in threats for 2025 Pride, hate-speech and intimidation risks persist.

sources.summary: Official Norwegian health-rights page (Gender Recognition Act): legal gender is determined by the individual's own perception of gender identity — self-declaration decided at the tax office — from age 16 alone, 6-16 with parents, under-6 only for documented congenital DSD; a 2017 regulation covers citizens resident abroad. For this record: the official, no-medical-intervention document-change route.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Norway: reported hate crimes rose 18% in 2023, with the largest increases in crimes motivated by sexual orientation, gender identity/expression and antisemitism; Zaniar Matapour sentenced to 30 years (the strictest penalty) for the 2022 Oslo Pride mass shooting; a drag bingo event sparked online threats; a knife attack on two people investigated as a hate crime.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (2020) covers Norway outlawing hate speech against trans people (amendment to the Penal Code).

NRK (May 2024, Norwegian): record numbers of hate-crime reports against queer and trans people in 2023, but the clearance rate fell from 52% to 45% and more cases were dropped; many victims report little trust in police, and a dedicated hate-crime group encourages reporting. For this record: rising reports with a documented, quantified drop in case clearance.

UiO C-REX research blog (Sept 2024): transphobic hostility in Norway manifests mainly among political extremists and religious fundamentalists — the Nordic Resistance Movement's 2017 Kristiansand march advocated 'crushing the gay lobby', and research interviews with far-right activists frame gender diversity as 'degeneracy'. For this record: organised ideological anti-trans hostility as a movement phenomenon, not street-level risk for ordinary visitors.

UiO C-REX (June 2025), HATECYCLE study of 3,000+ survey responses from LGBTQI people: only 8% of those who experienced a hate crime reported it to police — barriers include mistrust, procedural obstacles and fear of personal costs, and many who did report described dismissive treatment. For this record: official statistics undercount anti-LGBTQI hate crime by a wide margin.

OSCE/ODIHR frameworks page for Norway: hate crimes are defined as criminal offences motivated by hatred due to ethnicity, religion, belief, sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression, or disability; any offence so motivated is recorded under the framework. For this record: the statutory definition behind Norway's hate-crime counting.

Nordisk Post (Apr 2025): Norway's Police Security Service (PST) reports a 'significant decline' in threats against LGBTQ+ events and individuals over the past year, but warns hate speech and intimidation risks remain, especially during Pride — most threat actors aim to spread fear rather than act. For this record: current threat-level assessment from the security service.

records.name: Finland
records.summary: Finland is very safe for trans visitors. There are no documented severe trans-specific incidents (no tourist-rape, mob-violence or police-brutality case); bathrooms are unrestricted, there is no criminalisation, and the Schengen border poses no trans-specific friction. Record-level hate-crime reporting exists, but no incident series involving trans visitors is documented.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering 2025) chapter on Finland: record 1,808 suspected hate crimes in 2025 (+13% since 2023), with sexual orientation and gender identity recurrent motives (12% of cases); Finland's first conversion-practices case prosecuted as assault (convictions in March); Parliament endorsed a citizens' initiative to ban conversion practices (125-49) in March, though a full ban remained pending.

Finland's Police University College (Polamk, Nov 2025): record 1,808 suspected hate-crime offenses reported in 2024 — highest figure ever recorded; defamation and assault the most common types. The sexual-orientation/gender-identity-or-expression category climbed 72 -> 68 -> 126 -> 140 -> 215 -> 241 across the six reported years. The Criminal Code has no hate-crime category, so motive is only recorded in police reports — meaning SOGI-motivated incidents are counted via reported suspicion, not charge.

The Guardian (21 Mar 2025): Finland (with Denmark) updated its US travel advice for transgender citizens after reports of border ordeals following the US 'two genders' executive order — Denmark advises trans travellers to contact the US embassy in Copenhagen before departure over document issues. Signal for the record: Finland's government publicly sides with trans travellers facing document-based refusals abroad; issued as outbound advice, not destination risk.

Investigate Europe, 'The Cruel Condition' (10 Sep 2025): Finland, the Netherlands and Sweden explicitly wrote infertility requirements into law for legal gender recognition; at least 11,000 people subjected to such conditions across the six countries investigated, Sweden first (1972, in force 40 years); the last requirement was phased out at end-June 2025 — Finland's statutory sterilisation-era requirement is history, but the legacy cohort is documented.

Yle (28 Feb 2018): Parliament approved a citizens'-initiative-inspired change to the Maternity Act recognising both women in same-sex partnerships as mothers from the moment of the child's birth — second-parent registration fixed at birth rather than via adoption.

Yle (1 Mar 2017): same-sex marriage and joint adoption became legal in Finland; the western Finland register office alone had ~41 same-sex couples scheduled to marry in the first week — the operative date for all marriage-equality claims about Finland.

Yle (19 Sep 2013): the 'Tahdon2013' citizens' initiative for same-sex marriage collected 162,000+ certified signatures — largest Finnish initiative ever, far above the 50,000 threshold forcing parliamentary consideration; organiser target had been 250,000. The process route that produced the 2017 marriage law.

records.name: Taiwan
records.summary:
Taiwan is a progressive Asian destination — it was the first in Asia to legalise same-sex marriage (2019), the government is investing US$8.76 million to double gender-neutral public bathrooms by 2029, and a trans march in Taipei drew 3,000 participants in 2025. There are no documented severe incidents (no mob violence, trans-tourist rape, or organised dating-app predation).

The main gaps are legal-gender-recognition reform stagnation — a 2008 Ministry order still requires sex-reassignment surgery to change one's gender marker (blocking an estimated 90% of trans people, with only case-by-case court exceptions), and the government has been "floundering" on reform — and a rising anti-gender discourse movement that has produced online waves of hostility. A trans woman was outed during a police identity inspection (the Viva case), and Taipei has held a vigil for victims of anti-trans violence.

For a visitor, bathrooms are unrestricted (and being proactively expanded to gender-neutral), there is no criminalisation, and border/immigration poses no trans-specific friction. Ta

sources.summary: Taiwan Insight (Feb 2026): 'What about trans rights? Taiwan's ongoing struggle for self-ID' - the 2008 executive order requiring sex-reassignment surgery to change legal gender blocks an estimated 90% of trans people from obtaining matching national ID; every ID-requiring aspect of daily life (clinics, airport security) becomes a potential site of distress and discrimination; the Ministry of Health and Welfare has recognised gender self-determination as a human right since 2013.

Taiwan Insight (Jan 2026): the Taiwanese government continues to flounder on transgender rights in 2025 amidst continued transphobia - no tangible policy change on abolishing the surgery requirement or expanding assisted reproduction; pending conscription-criteria changes could actively harm trans people; anti-gender movement activity rising, with organisations supporting Trump's anti-trans policies and the Taiwan Solidarity Party calling for a 'two genders' position.

Taipei Times (Aug 2024): the Ministry of Environment will invest NT$280 million over four years to double gender-neutral public bathrooms nationwide (623 to 1,246 by 2029); of trans and gender-neutral survey respondents reporting discrimination, 17% occurred in public restrooms or changing rooms.

Focus Taiwan (Nov 2025): 'Most Taiwan all-gender restrooms do not meet standards: Rights group' — an LGBTQ+ rights group finds only 5 of 149 government-listed all-gender toilets met the required standards, including clear all-gender signage.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 404 - page removed); the underlying page addressed Taiwan's transgender rights - laws, protections and gaps.
New Bloom (Nov 2024): analysis of the wave of anti-gender discourse in Taiwan - rising anti-gender movement activity and its political context.

TaiwanPlus (Aug 2024): a Taipei court denied a transgender woman's request to change the gender marker on her government ID without requiring surgery or a psychological evaluation; the supporting rights group says they will likely appeal.

JURIST dispatch (Nov 2025): the 7th annual Taiwan Transgender March in Taipei drew an estimated 3,000 people despite rain, with international participants; calls for an end to discrimination against trans people as the rights debate continues.

records.name: South Korea
records.summary: South Korea is broadly workable for trans visitors — there is no criminalisation, courts have protected trans people's restroom access and ruled favourably on legal gender recognition, and Seoul hosts one of Asia's largest Pride parades. There is no same-sex marriage, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner, and no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering services. No severe incidents involving trans visitors are documented. Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods are welcoming; outside them, more caution is warranted.

sources.summary: Seoul Central District Court, final 2 Jul 2024 (no appeal): police advising a trans plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights; symbolic compensation of 300,000 won against the state, recognising the infringement.

Yonhap (8 May 2024): a court (Yeongdong) ruled against mandating sex-reassignment surgery to change legal sex status — five plaintiffs assigned male at birth, on hormone therapy for years; the court held demanding surgery violates physical integrity and that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals.

The Hankyoreh (21 Mar 2024): youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong research presented 20 Mar 2024 shows trans teens avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed — a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reports holding it in and leaving school early; researchers urged law and institutional reforms for safer school environments.

Korea Herald (28 Nov 2023): the state human rights watchdog NHRCK flagged a 'transgender blind spot in hospitalisation' — the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, saying accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): civilian same-sex conduct legal but criminalised in the military under Military Criminal Act Art. 92-6, upheld by the Constitutional Court in 2023; legal gender recognition possible; no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity; LGBTI organisations can register.

Peer-reviewed nationwide survey (Epidemiology and Health, 27 Jun 2025): 585 transgender and non-binary young adults mapped key milestones and stigmatization across life stages — documents pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care.

HRW World Report 2025, South Korea chapter (events of 2024): overall relatively positive record with free media and civil society, but persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people; chapter also covers the December 2024 martial-law crisis and assembly freedoms.

misterb&b gay travel guide to South Korea safety (July 2026): broadly positive for visitors to Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighborhoods but requiring contextual understanding - military-law criminalisation, organised conservative opposition, no national anti-discrimination law, alongside rapid social change and a landmark 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights.

records.name: China
records.summary:
China demands real caution — authoritarian but not criminalising: there is no criminalisation of trans identity, no bathroom-restriction law, and courts can provide some protection, but there are no anti-discrimination protections. The most directly visitor-specific finding is airport discrimination: a Thai trans YouTuber was singled out and subjected to discriminatory treatment at a Chinese airport. Displaying rainbow symbols inside venues has been disallowed — relevant to a visitor planning visible expression — and a foreign drag queen's tour was cancelled, showing foreign gender-nonconforming performers can meet repression while working here.

The most severe documented case — forced psychiatric commitment with electroshock 'conversion' therapy under family pressure, where a resident won unprecedented compensation — targeted a resident, not a tourist, showing the medical system can be weaponised; it does not scale directly to a visitor.

sources.summary: The Thaiger (27 May 2025): Thai trans YouTuber Nisamanee 'Nut' Lertvorapong alleged Chinese immigration officials laughed at, mocked and questioned her during a family trip, posting video on Instagram with 'No one should be treated differently, no matter what their gender is.' Direct visitor-facing evidence of how a visibly trans traveller was treated at a Chinese border post.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying NYT investigation (Dec 2024) covers transgender 'conversion' practices in China.

The Guardian (21 Nov 2024): performance artist Ling'er, 28, won a record monetary payout after being subjected to electroshock 'conversion' treatment — the first time a trans person had successfully challenged such treatment in China; she said she hoped the case would help other LGBTQ+ people protect their rights.

Human Rights Watch (25 Jun 2026): around Pride month, platforms scrubbed prominent LGBT social media accounts, foreign films and events with LGBT themes — HRW reads the censorship wave as illustrating a deteriorating rights situation for LGBT people in China (deepening repression restricting expression and association).

Radio Free Asia (28 Jan 2024): the CCP's crackdown against 'foreign ideologies' has made LGBTQ+ activism 'all but extinct' on the mainland — displaying rainbow flags or accessories is no longer allowed even inside venues, and in August 2023 officials removed an LGBTQ+ anthem titled 'Rainbow'. Ongoing harassment of queer expression in public space.

Foreign Policy (Jan 2025): gender transition in China is treated as 'a family affair' — even adults need parental consent to undergo gender-affirming surgery and change their legal gender (and must prove parental death if applicable); families are forced to resolve disagreements about the procedure internally. Practical barriers to care for trans residents and long-stay visitors.

Outright International overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): China's long-standing 'don't encourage, don't oppose, don't promote' posture has grown restrictive — the Cybersecurity Law and related rules censor LGBTI content deemed to 'disrupt social order'; LGBTI organisations cannot register, legal gender recognition is unavailable, and same-sex conduct has no legal protection.

CNN (3 Jan 2025): cancellation of nationwide shows by famous transgender dancer Jin Xing led some in China to fear a wider LGBTQ+ crackdown — the case of China's most visible trans star becoming a bellwether for the tightening climate.
